name: Sts. Jacinta and Francisco Marto, and the Fatima tree
title: Shepherd children, seers of Fatima
feast: 20 February (where kept; not on the General Roman Calendar)
summary: Francisco and Jacinta Marto were shepherd children of Fatima, in Portugal, who with their cousin Lúcia said that a lady from heaven appeared to them in 1917. Both died young in the influenza epidemic after the First World War, and they were canonized for how they lived, not for what they saw. Popular devotion asks their prayers for sick children and for peace, and they show the Prep's youngest students that holiness does not wait for adulthood.
life: Francisco and Jacinta Marto were brother and sister, the youngest children of a farming family in Aljustrel, a hamlet in the parish of Fatima in central Portugal. Like most children of the village they could not read, and they spent their days minding the family's sheep with their older cousin, Lúcia dos Santos. Francisco was quiet and liked to be alone. Jacinta was lively and quick to cry.

In 1917 the three children said that a lady from heaven appeared to them over a small holm oak (in Portuguese azinheira) at the Cova da Iria, a hollow where they grazed the sheep. She came on the 13th of each month from May to October, except in August, when the local administrator held the children and the meeting took place a few days later elsewhere. Lúcia later wrote that the lady asked them to pray the rosary every day, to pray and make sacrifices for sinners, and to pray for peace. Francisco saw the lady but did not hear her words. On 13 October a large crowd said they saw the sun spin and plunge. The children were questioned, threatened and doubted, and people came by the thousands. Within months pilgrims had stripped the little tree bare for keepsakes.

The two younger children took the message to heart in different ways. Francisco spent hours praying alone, wanting, as he put it, to console the hidden Jesus in the tabernacle. Jacinta was moved most by the thought of sinners and gave up food and water on hot days for them. Both caught the influenza that swept Europe after the First World War. Francisco died at home on 4 April 1919, not yet eleven. Jacinta suffered for months, was taken to a hospital in Lisbon, and died there alone on 20 February 1920, aged nine. Lúcia became a nun and lived until 2005.

The bishop of Leiria approved the apparitions in 1930 as worthy of belief. That is approval of a private revelation. It means the Church finds nothing in it against faith and allows devotion to it, but no Catholic is bound to believe it. The holiness of the two children is a separate matter, judged by their lives. John Paul II beatified them at Fatima in 2000, and Pope Francis canonized them there on 13 May 2017. They are the youngest saints who were not martyrs.
patronage: sick children and the sick (popular devotion)
children who pray for peace (popular devotion)
why_here: Jacinta and Francisco were canonized for how they lived as children, not for having seen something. That is a useful thing for the Prep's youngest students, seventh and eighth graders, to hear: holiness is not something that waits until you are grown. Francisco's habit of slipping away to sit before the tabernacle is close to what the monks do in their church day after day, and it is open to any student who walks across to the abbey church.

They also died in the influenza epidemic that followed the First World War. In 1918 the same disease killed Frater Hubert Carney of this abbey while he was nursing others. The Fatima children and the young monk are a reminder that the epidemics of the past took the young and the generous first, and a reason to pray for the sick in the abbey's infirmary and in students' families.
relic: One steel pendant on the grey linen board with three relics labelled "HYACINTHAE", "FRANCISCI" and "ARBORIS": of Jacinta, of Francisco, and of the tree, most likely the Fatima holm oak.
check: The labels do not say "Fatima"; the reading rests on the three names together. The two have no official patronage that I could confirm, so the patronages given are popular devotion only. "Youngest non-martyr saints" is the usual claim; worth a quick check before publishing.

name: St. Joachim
title: Father of the Virgin Mary
summary: Joachim is the name tradition gives to the father of the Virgin Mary. The Bible does not mention him, and his story comes from the Protoevangelium of James, a second-century writing the Church never took as Scripture. He is a patron of fathers and grandparents, and he stands for the parents and grandparents who make the Prep possible and for the patient, waiting prayer a monastery is built on.
life: The Bible says nothing about the parents of the Virgin Mary. Their names, Joachim and Anne, come from the Protoevangelium of James, a Greek writing of the second century that tells the story of Mary's birth and childhood. The Church never accepted it as Scripture, and much of it is plainly pious storytelling, but its names and some of its scenes passed into the prayer and art of both East and West.

In that story Joachim is a rich and devout man of Israel who gives a double share of his goods, one part to the people and one to God. When he comes to the Temple with his offering, he is turned away because he has no children in Israel. Ashamed, he does not go home but goes into the desert, pitches his tent and fasts for forty days and nights. Meanwhile Anne mourns at home. An angel comes to each of them and says that they will have a child. Joachim returns with his flocks, Anne runs to meet him at the gate, and they embrace. That meeting at the Golden Gate became one of the best loved scenes in medieval painting, most famously by Giotto in Padua.

The same story says Mary was born to them, and that when she was three they brought her to the Temple to be raised there. Nothing more is told of Joachim. Later writers guessed at his age and death, but no one knows them.

His cult began in the East, where he and Anne have been honored together for many centuries. In the West his feast came later and moved several times before 1969, when it was joined to Anne's on 26 July. What the Church honors in him is not the details of the legend, which no one is asked to believe, but the plain fact behind it: Mary had a father, and the faith she brought to the Annunciation was first taught her at home.
why_here: Joachim's story is that of a father and grandfather nobody remembers by name in the Bible, whose quiet faith shaped what came after. Many of the people who make St. Bernard Prep possible are like him: the fathers who drive a boarder hundreds of miles in August, and the grandparents who help pay tuition or pray for a grandchild far from home. His feast with Anne falls in late July, close to the Church's World Day for Grandparents, before the school year begins.
For the monks he is a figure of patience. Joachim went into the desert to pray when his hopes had come to nothing, and waited. A monastery is built on that kind of waiting prayer.
relic: One relic on the grey linen board, labelled "Oss. S. Ioachin C.", "bones of St. Joachim, Confessor"; any bone relic of him rests on tradition only.
check: The World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly (begun by Pope Francis in 2021) is kept on the fourth Sunday of July, near this feast; confirm before publishing if that line is kept.

name: St. John Berchmans
title: Jesuit student, patron of altar servers
summary: John Berchmans was a young Flemish Jesuit who died in Rome in 1621 at twenty-two, still a student. He did nothing outwardly remarkable, but he kept the ordinary rules of his house exactly and cheerfully. He is a patron of altar servers and students, and a natural friend to Prep boarders who live by a timetable far from home, and to monks whose day is set by the bell.
life: John Berchmans was born in 1599 at Diest, a small town in Brabant, in what is now Belgium. His father was a shoemaker who later, after his wife died, became a priest. John was the eldest son, a serious, good-humored boy who served Mass in the town churches from an early age. To pay for his schooling he worked as a servant in the house of a priest in Mechelen.

In 1616, at seventeen, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Mechelen, against the hopes of his father, who had counted on him to help the family. Two years later he was sent on foot to Rome to study philosophy at the Roman College. He was a good student and liked his studies, and he took part in the public disputations that were the examinations of the time.

He did nothing outwardly remarkable. What struck those who lived with him was that he kept the ordinary rules of the house, the timetable, the silences, the small courtesies, exactly and cheerfully, day after day. A saying is attributed to him that the common life was his greatest penance. He wrote down short resolutions and kept them, and he was known for his devotion to Mary.

In August 1621, soon after a disputation, he fell ill with a fever, probably made worse by overwork in the Roman summer. He died on 13 August, aged twenty-two, holding his crucifix, his rosary and his book of rules, and saying that these were the three things dearest to him. He had not yet been ordained. He is buried in the church of Sant'Ignazio in Rome, near St. Aloysius Gonzaga.

He was beatified in 1865. One of the miracles accepted for his canonization was the healing in 1866 of Mary Wilson, a young novice at the Academy of the Sacred Heart in Grand Coteau, Louisiana, a boarding school. Leo XIII canonized him in 1888. He is a patron of altar servers and of young people at their studies.
why_here: John Berchmans was a student who lived by a timetable, among others, far from home, and became a saint by doing the ordinary things of that life well. That describes a boarder at St. Bernard Prep closely. His holiness was not in great deeds but in getting up on time, studying, being kind to the people in the next room, and praying. He is a fitting patron for the Prep's students and for those who serve at the altar in the abbey church.

He would also understand the monks. A Benedictine's day is set by the bell and the horarium, and the Rule asks for the same faithfulness in small things that John practiced. One of his miracles happened at a Catholic boarding school in the American South.
relic: One relic in a sunburst stand, labelled "s. Joan. Berch", one of the four matching stands with Sts. Aloysius Gonzaga, Camillus de Lellis and Paul of the Cross.
check: The saying about the common life (maxima mea poenitentia vita communis) is traditionally attributed to him; confirm wording if quoted.

name: St. John Bosco
title: Priest, educator, founder of the Salesians
summary: John Bosco was a nineteenth-century priest of Turin who gathered poor boys off the streets, gave them schools and workshops, and founded the Salesians to carry on the work. He taught by reason, religion and loving kindness rather than fear. He is a patron of young people, students and educators, the name saint of Fr. John, and close to the Prep's own aim of a love of learning and a life of virtue.
life: Giovanni Bosco was born on 16 August 1815 at Becchi, a hamlet near Castelnuovo d'Asti in Piedmont, in northern Italy. His father died when he was two, and his mother, Margherita, raised three boys on a small farm. John later said that at about nine he had a dream in which he was among a crowd of fighting, swearing boys, and was told he must win them not with blows but with gentleness and kindness. To draw the village boys to hear the catechism he taught himself juggling, acrobatics and conjuring tricks, and at the end of each show he repeated the Sunday sermon.

He was poor and had to work his way through school, as a farmhand, a tailor's help, a waiter and a blacksmith's apprentice, among other things. He was ordained in Turin in 1841. Turin was then filling with country boys looking for work in the new factories and building sites. Many slept rough, and many ended up in prison. Don Bosco visited the prisons and decided that the young needed help before they got there.

He began gathering boys on Sundays for play, Mass and catechism. After years of moving from place to place, his oratory settled in 1846 at Valdocco, on the edge of the city. His mother came to live there and keep house. He took in boys who had nowhere to sleep, opened night classes and then a school, and set up workshops where boys learned to be shoemakers, tailors, bookbinders, carpenters and printers. He wrote and printed books for ordinary readers, and he built the large church of Mary Help of Christians, consecrated in 1868.

His method, which he called the preventive system, rested on reason, religion and loving kindness. Teachers were to live among the boys, at play as well as in class, so that rules were kept out of trust rather than fear, and punishment was rarely needed. To carry on the work he founded the Salesians, named for St. Francis de Sales, and in 1872, with St. Mary Mazzarello, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, for girls. Before he died there were Salesian houses in Europe and South America.

Many stories of prophetic dreams and wonders were told about him, some recorded by his followers. He died worn out in Turin on 31 January 1888. Pius XI, who had met him as a young priest, beatified him in 1929 and canonized him on Easter Sunday 1934. In 1988 John Paul II called him Father and Teacher of Youth.
why_here: Don Bosco is the name saint of Fr. John, and he is perhaps the best patron St. Bernard Prep could have. He ran something very like a boarding school, for boys who were far from home, and he insisted that the teachers belong to the boys' whole day, the playground as much as the classroom. At the Prep the monks teach, coach, keep the library and say Mass for the students. That is the preventive system in another form, and the school's aim, "cultivating a love of learning and a life of virtue in young men and women", is close to his own.

He would also recognize the abbey's workshops. He taught boys trades and ran a press, and the abbey keeps a tradition of craftsman monks and publishes its own books. His prayers belong to every teacher who has to choose between patience and punishment.
relic: One relic in a gilt cross-shaped stand with red and green stones, labelled "B. Ioann. Bosco C.", which calls him Blessed and so was written between 1929 and 1934.
check: Patronage of editors and publishers is often said to have been declared by a pope (Pius XII is sometimes named); I left the pope out because I could not confirm it.

name: St. John Neumann
title: Redemptorist, Bishop of Philadelphia
summary: John Neumann was a German-speaking priest from Bohemia who came to America in 1836, joined the Redemptorists and became Bishop of Philadelphia. There he built the first diocesan Catholic school system in the country. A patron of Catholic schools and of immigrants, he shares the abbey's German immigrant roots, and he is a good saint to ask for the Prep's teachers and its future.
life: John Nepomucene Neumann was born on 28 March 1811 at Prachatitz (Prachatice) in Bohemia, then part of the Austrian Empire and now in the Czech Republic. His father was a German stocking-maker, his mother Czech, and he grew up speaking both languages. He studied at the seminary in Budweis and at the university in Prague, and he had a gift for languages that he kept adding to all his life.

When his studies were done in 1835, his bishop was not ordaining more priests because the diocese had too many. Neumann had read the letters of missionaries in America, so he set out on his own, with little money, and landed in New York in 1836. Bishop John Dubois ordained him within weeks and sent him to the German-speaking settlers around Buffalo and Niagara Falls, a huge, poor parish that he covered mostly on foot.

Lonely and exhausted, he joined the Redemptorists in 1840 and in 1842 became the first of them to make vows in the United States. He worked in their German parishes in Baltimore and Pittsburgh and became their superior in America. In 1852 he was named Bishop of Philadelphia.

Philadelphia was a large diocese full of new immigrants. Neumann built churches at the rate of nearly one a month and gave his greatest effort to schools. He organized the parish schools under a central board, the first diocesan Catholic school system in the country, and in a few years their number grew from a handful to nearly a hundred. He brought in religious sisters and brothers to teach, and he learned enough Italian, Irish Gaelic and other languages to hear confessions from his people. He also organized the Forty Hours devotion across the diocese. Some in Philadelphia thought him too plain and too foreign for a big city, but he went on as he was.

On 5 January 1860, walking in the street on an errand, he collapsed and died, aged forty-eight. Paul VI beatified him in 1963 and canonized him in 1977, the first American bishop to be made a saint. His body is in the church of St. Peter the Apostle in Philadelphia.
why_here: Neumann is a patron the abbey has every reason to love. He was a German-speaking priest from Central Europe who came to serve German-speaking Catholics in America, as the monks of Metten and St. Vincent did, and as the monks who came to Cullman, a town founded by German immigrants, did after them. He worked for a time in Pittsburgh, not far from St. Vincent Archabbey.

Above all he believed that immigrant Catholics needed their own schools, and he spent himself building them. The monks have taught in Alabama since 1892, in one kind of school after another, and St. Bernard Prep is a Catholic school in the line he helped start. He is a good patron to ask for the teachers and for the school's future.
relic: One relic on the grey linen board, labelled "[E]x Oss. S. Jo. Neumann", "from the bones of St. John Neumann"; it calls him Saint, so the label is from 1977 or later.
check: The figures for Philadelphia's schools (from two or a handful to about a hundred) and churches (nearly one a month) are the usual ones in his biographies; confirm if exact numbers are wanted.

name: St. John the Baptist
title: Prophet, the Forerunner of Christ
summary: John the Baptist, son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, preached repentance in the desert, baptized Jesus in the Jordan and pointed him out as the Lamb of God, and Herod Antipas had him beheaded. He is a patron of the baptized and of monks and hermits. The monks sing his father's Benedictus every morning, and teachers can learn from his habit of pointing beyond himself.
life: John is the only saint besides Mary whose birth the Church keeps as a feast. Luke's Gospel tells that he was the son of the elderly priest Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, Mary's kinswoman. An angel announced his birth to Zechariah in the Temple, and when Zechariah doubted he was struck dumb until the child was named. Then he sang the hymn that begins "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel", the Benedictus. When the pregnant Mary visited Elizabeth, the unborn John leapt in his mother's womb.

As a grown man John lived in the desert of Judea, dressed in camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He preached repentance and baptized crowds in the Jordan as a sign of turning back to God. He had disciples of his own, and some of them, Andrew among them, left him to follow Jesus. He baptized Jesus, and he pointed him out with the words "Behold the Lamb of God", which are still said at every Mass. Jesus said that no one born of woman was greater than John.

John condemned Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, for marrying Herodias, the wife of his brother. Herod put him in prison in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. The Gospels tell how Herodias's daughter danced at Herod's birthday feast and, prompted by her mother, asked for John's head on a dish. The Jewish historian Josephus also writes of John's preaching and of his death at Herod's order, though he gives a political reason for it.

His relics were venerated by the fourth century, and many churches, east and west, claim parts of them, more than one of them his head. Whether any one of these old relics is truly his is a question for history, not for faith. The Church calls him the Forerunner, Praecursor, the one who went before Christ to prepare his way, and he is the last of the prophets.
why_here: John belongs in a monastery. He went into the desert to pray and to live simply, and the early monks saw him as one of their models. St. Gregory the Great tells that when St. Benedict came to Monte Cassino he pulled down the altar of Apollo and built a chapel of St. John the Baptist in its place. Every morning at Lauds the monks of St. Bernard sing the Benedictus, the hymn of John's father at his birth.

There is a choir link too. The old hymn for his feast, Ut queant laxis, gave the Benedictine monk Guido of Arezzo the names of the notes, ut (do), re, mi, fa, sol, la. John is also a model for teachers. His whole work was to point beyond himself, "He must increase, I must decrease", which is what a good teacher does for a student.
relic: Two relics: one labelled "S. Joann. Bapt." in the velvet case, sharing a theca with the tomb of Our Lady, and one on the grey linen board labelled "Jo. Bapt. Prae[cursoris]", "of John the Baptist, the Forerunner".
check: Patron of French Canadians: declared by Pius X in 1908, as I recall; please confirm the pope and year.

name: St. John Vianney
title: The Curé of Ars, parish priest
summary: John Vianney, the Curé of Ars, was a French farm boy who nearly failed in the seminary because he could not learn Latin. As priest of a small village he spent up to sixteen hours a day hearing the confessions of crowds from all over France. Pius XI named him patron of parish priests, and he is a friend to the abbey's priests and to any Prep student struggling with Latin.
life: Jean-Marie Vianney was born on 8 May 1786 at Dardilly, near Lyon, the son of farmers. He grew up during the French Revolution, when the Church was persecuted. He made his first Communion in secret, at a farmhouse with the windows covered, and the priests he knew were men who said Mass in hiding. He worked on the farm as a boy and had very little schooling.

He was nearly twenty when he began studying for the priesthood, under Fr. Charles Balley, the parish priest of nearby Écully. He found study, and Latin above all, terribly hard. In 1809 he was called up for Napoleon's army, fell ill, missed his unit, and ended up hiding for more than a year in a mountain village as a deserter, until an amnesty freed him. At the seminary he failed his examinations and was nearly sent home. Fr. Balley vouched for his goodness, and he was ordained in 1815 at twenty-nine.

In 1818 he was sent to Ars, a village of a couple of hundred people north of Lyon, where religion had fallen away. He prayed for hours in the church, ate little, gave away nearly everything, visited every family, and preached plainly against drinking, dancing and working on Sundays. He opened a home for orphaned and poor girls called the Providence. Slowly the village changed.

Then people began coming from elsewhere to confess to him, first from the next villages, then from all over France. By the 1830s tens of thousands came every year, and a special railway ticket to Ars was sold at Lyon. He spent eleven to sixteen hours a day in the confessional, in a cold church in winter and a stifling one in summer. He was known for reading hearts and for kindness to the despairing. He told of being harassed at night by the devil, and many stories of wonders grew up around him. Three times he tried to run away to a monastery, and each time he came back.
He died at Ars on 4 August 1859, worn out at seventy-three. He was canonized in 1925, and in 1929 Pius XI named him patron of parish priests.
why_here: Students at St. Bernard Prep who struggle with Latin have a friend in the Curé of Ars. He nearly lost his vocation because he could not learn it, and he became a saint anyway. He is a patron for any student who is slow at something and tempted to give up, and for the monks who teach Latin and have to be patient with them.

He is also a patron for the abbey's priests. Several monks have served as pastors, and at the abbey they hear confessions, say Mass for the students and receive guests at the Retreat Center. John Vianney wanted all his life to be a monk and was never allowed to be one. His prayers for those who are both may be especially kind.
relic: Two relics on the grey linen board: one labelled "S. Ioann. M. Vian[ney]", and one in a gilt pendant he shares with St. Philip Neri and St. Catherine Labouré.

name: St. Joseph
title: Spouse of the Virgin Mary, craftsman of Nazareth
feast: 19 March; St. Joseph the Worker, 1 May
summary: Joseph, the just man of Nazareth, took Mary as his wife, protected the child Jesus and taught him a craftsman's trade, and the Gospels record no word from him. He is patron of the Universal Church, of workers and of a happy death. He belongs in a house of craftsman monks, whose best-known builder, Br. Joseph Zoettl, bore his name.
life: Almost everything we know of Joseph comes from the first chapters of Matthew and Luke. He was of the house of David, living at Nazareth in Galilee and engaged to Mary. Matthew calls him a just man. When he found that Mary was with child, he decided to end the engagement quietly, to spare her shame, until an angel told him in a dream to take her as his wife. He did, and gave the child his name and his place in David's line.

Joseph went with Mary to Bethlehem for the census, and Jesus was born there. Warned in another dream, he took the mother and child by night and fled to Egypt to escape Herod's killing of the children, and he brought them back only when told it was safe. Each time, the Gospels record no word from him, only that he got up and did what he was told. He settled the family in Nazareth. When Jesus was twelve, Joseph and Mary lost him on the way home from Jerusalem and found him after three days in the Temple. After that Joseph is not mentioned again, and he probably died before Jesus began to preach.

The Gospels call Jesus "the carpenter's son". The Greek word, tekton, means a builder or craftsman who worked in wood and perhaps in stone. Jesus learned the trade from him and was himself called "the carpenter". Joseph earned his family's bread with his hands.

No one knows where he was buried, so there are no known bones of St. Joseph. Relics of him are said to be of his cloak or belt. Devotion to him grew slowly, through the Middle Ages, and then quickly. St. Teresa of Ávila spread it widely. Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870, Pius XII set his feast as St. Joseph the Worker on 1 May in 1955, and John XXIII added his name to the Roman Canon. Because tradition says he died with Jesus and Mary beside him, he became the patron of a happy death.
why_here: Joseph was a craftsman, and St. Bernard Abbey is a house of craftsman monks. The abbey's builders, carvers and woodworkers, who make altars, pews, doors and furniture, practice his trade. The man who made the abbey best known, Br. Joseph Zoettl, carried his name, and spent decades building the 125 small shrines of the Ave Maria Grotto from stone, shells and scrap. The Benedictine motto, prayer and work, could stand under any picture of the house at Nazareth.

He is also the patron of a happy death. The abbey keeps an infirmary for its old and sick monks and a cemetery where they lie. For the Prep he is a father who raised a son he did not beget and taught him a trade, a good patron for the teachers, dorm parents and coaches who stand in for fathers far away.
relic: Three relics: one on the grey linen board labelled "s, Joseph. Sp[onsi]", one in the velvet case's square theca labelled "s. Josephi Sp.", and one in the large oval of fifteen labelled "s. Jos. Sp. V. M."; with no known tomb, such relics are said to be of his cloak or belt.
check: The catalogue reads the label "s. Jos. Sp. V. M." in the oval of fifteen as St. Joseph, Spouse of the Virgin Mary; Br. Augustine may want to confirm I have counted three Joseph relics correctly.

name: St. Jude Thaddeus
title: Apostle
summary: Jude Thaddeus was one of the Twelve Apostles and speaks once in the Gospels, at the Last Supper. Nothing certain is known of his later life, though Western tradition says he was martyred in Persia with St. Simon. He is the patron of hopeless cases, the saint of families and students who have run out of options, and the name saint of the abbey's carver, Br. Jude.
life: Jude is one of the Twelve, though the Gospels name him in different ways. Luke, in his Gospel and in Acts, calls him "Judas son of James". Matthew and Mark have no Judas in that place in their lists, but a Thaddaeus, and the Church has long taken them to be the same man. He speaks once in the Gospels. At the Last Supper, John writes, "Judas, not Iscariot" asked Jesus why he would show himself to the disciples and not to the world, and Jesus answered that he and the Father would come and make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word.

The short Letter of Jude in the New Testament is by "Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James". It warns against false teachers and ends with a well known blessing. Tradition credits it to the apostle, but many scholars think it was written by another Jude, perhaps a relative of Jesus, and the question is open.

Nothing certain is known of his later life. Different traditions send him to preach in Syria, Mesopotamia, Persia and Armenia, and the Armenian Church honors him and St. Bartholomew as its first apostles. Western tradition says he was martyred in Persia with St. Simon, and that is why the two share a feast. Some old stories also mixed him up with Addai, or Thaddeus, the missionary who in legend brought King Abgar of Edessa a cloth with the face of Christ, which is why he is often shown with a medallion of that face. Relics said to be his and Simon's are in St. Peter's Basilica.

Through most of history he was little prayed to. It is often said that his name, so like that of Judas Iscariot, kept people away, so that they turned to him only when nothing else had worked. Whatever the reason, devotion to him as patron of hopeless cases grew strong from the nineteenth century, and he became one of the most popular saints in America.
patronage: hospitals and the seriously ill (popular devotion)
why_here: The abbey's carver, Br. Jude, bears his name, and the relic sits in a brass cross of its own, set apart from the larger groups. Jude is the saint of people who have run out of options: a family facing a frightening diagnosis, a student whose year has gone badly wrong, a parent worried about a child far away. Many such prayers are sent to monasteries, with Mass intentions and novenas, because people trust that monks will keep praying when they themselves are too tired.

His one question at the Last Supper is also a good one for a school. He asked why Jesus would not show himself to everyone. The answer, that God makes his home with those who love him, is a fair description of what a monastery is trying to be.
relic: One relic in a brass reliquary cross, labelled "S. J. Thaddaei A.", "of St. Jude Thaddeus, Apostle".

name: St. Justina
title: Virgin and martyr (which Justina is not known)
feast: Unknown, since the saint is unknown (St. Justina of Padua, 7 October)
summary: The label reads only "of Saint Justina, Virgin and Martyr", and several early saints fit it, so which Justina this is is not known. The best known, Justina of Padua, is a martyr whose life is legend but whose cult is very old, and she is a patron of Padua and Venice. If it is she, the reform begun at her abbey grew into the Cassinese Congregation, and St. Bernard belongs to the American-Cassinese Congregation.
life: The label "S. Iustinae V.M." means "of Saint Justina, Virgin and Martyr", and several early saints of the name fit it. The best known is St. Justina of Padua, said to have been a young Christian of that city martyred around 304 in the persecution of Diocletian. The account of her life was written much later and is legend, but her cult is very old. The great Benedictine abbey of Santa Giustina was built over her tomb in Padua, and in the fifteenth century its abbot Ludovico Barbo led a reform that spread to many Italian monasteries as the Congregation of Santa Giustina. When Monte Cassino joined it, it became the Cassinese Congregation. The Venetians took her as a patron after the victory of Lepanto, which was won on her feast day in 1571.

Another candidate is St. Justina of Antioch, who in legend converted the magician Cyprian, a man who had tried to win her by sorcery, and was martyred with him. That story is a pious romance and was taken off the general calendar in 1969. There were other martyrs named Justina too, in Rome and elsewhere, about whom almost nothing is known. Without the reliquary's papers, the label does not say which Justina this is.
why_here: If this is Justina of Padua, she has a real tie to this house. The monastic reform that began at her abbey grew into the Cassinese Congregation, and St. Bernard belongs to the American-Cassinese Congregation, founded by the monks of St. Vincent. Her abbey in Padua also keeps the body of St. Luke, whose relic is here too. Whichever Justina she is, she stands for the young women martyrs of the early Church, whose courage the Prep's girls can claim as their own.
relic: One relic in the wooden box with a glass front, with Sts. Agapitus and Secundus, labelled (likely) "S. Iustinae V. M.".
check: Which Justina is meant can only be settled by the authentica. Also confirm the history of the name: the American-Cassinese Congregation took its name and constitutions from the Cassinese Congregation; I have only said it belongs to it.

name: St. Lawrence
title: Deacon of Rome, martyr
summary: Lawrence was a deacon of Rome who cared for the Church's goods and its poor, and he was put to death in 258, days after Pope Sixtus II. The story that he presented the poor as the Church's treasures and was roasted on a gridiron was told a century later and may be legend. He is a patron of deacons, the poor, cooks and librarians, which suits a house with a library and a bakery.
life: Lawrence was one of the seven deacons of the Church of Rome in the middle of the third century. Deacons in Rome looked after the Church's money and property and its care for the poor, the widows and the sick, and Lawrence seems to have been the chief of them. A later tradition says he came from Spain, but nothing sure is known of his early life.

In 257 the Emperor Valerian began a hard persecution aimed at the Church's leaders and its property. In August 258 Pope Sixtus II was arrested while celebrating the liturgy in a catacomb and beheaded with several of his deacons. Lawrence was put to death on 10 August, a few days later. These facts and the dates are firm. Lawrence was buried on the Via Tiburtina, and Constantine built a church over his tomb, the forerunner of the basilica of San Lorenzo outside the Walls.

The rest of the story was told about a century later, by St. Ambrose and the poet Prudentius. Ambrose writes that Lawrence wept to be left behind by Sixtus, and that Sixtus told him he would follow in three days. Ordered by the prefect of Rome to hand over the Church's treasures, Lawrence asked for time, gathered the poor, the blind and the lame, and presented them, saying, "These are the treasures of the Church". He was then roasted alive on a gridiron, and, the story goes, told his executioners, "Turn me over, this side is done". Many historians think that, like Sixtus, he was in fact beheaded, and that the gridiron came from a slip in an early text or from the storytellers. The answer about the poor, though, sums up a real deacon's work.
He was one of the most honored martyrs of Rome. His name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass. The meteor showers that peak around his feast are still called the Tears of St. Lawrence in Italy.
patronage: comedians (from his joke on the gridiron)
why_here: Lawrence is a patron of librarians and archivists because he kept the Church's goods and records, and a patron of cooks because of the gridiron. Both have a place here. Br. Thomas keeps the abbey library, and Br. Leo keeps its history in print. The kitchen and the bakery feed thirty monks, guests and students.

His answer about the poor is the one to remember. A monastery owns land, buildings and things of value, this reliquary among them, and the Rule tells the monks to treat the tools of the house like the vessels of the altar. Lawrence is a reminder of what all of it is for. He and St. Sebastian, both young martyrs of Rome, keep each other company here in a matching pair of sunbursts.
relic: One relic in a small sunburst, labelled "[S.] Laurentii Lev. M", "of St. Lawrence, Deacon and Martyr", one of a matching pair with St. Sebastian.
check: Patron of comedians is a popular, not official, patronage; drop it if it seems too light for the page.

name: St. Leonard of Port Maurice
title: Franciscan preacher of the Way of the Cross
summary: Leonard of Port Maurice was an Italian Franciscan who preached parish missions across Italy for more than forty years. His great cause was the Way of the Cross, which he set up hundreds of times, in the Colosseum among other places. He is patron of parish missions, and his pilgrimage for those who cannot reach Jerusalem is the same idea that lies behind the Ave Maria Grotto.
life: Paolo Girolamo Casanova was born on 20 December 1676 at Porto Maurizio, a small port on the Ligurian coast of Italy, the son of a sea captain. At thirteen he was sent to an uncle in Rome and studied at the Jesuits' Roman College, where he did well. His family wanted him to become a doctor. Instead, in 1697, he joined the Franciscans of the strict Reformed branch and took the name Leonard.

After his ordination he fell seriously ill, with bleeding from the lungs that seemed to be tuberculosis, and was sent home to Porto Maurizio to recover. He promised that if he got well he would give his life to preaching. He recovered and kept the promise for more than forty years.

Leonard became the best known preacher of parish missions in Italy. A mission was a week or two of sermons, confessions and processions meant to wake up a whole town or district. He preached hundreds of them, through Tuscany, the Papal States, Genoa, and as far as Corsica, walking from place to place, often outdoors before huge crowds. He was gentle in the confessional and fierce in the pulpit. He wrote a short book on the Mass, The Hidden Treasure, which is still in print, and he promoted devotion to the Sacred Heart, to the Blessed Sacrament and to the Immaculate Conception.

His great cause was the Way of the Cross. The Stations, a way of walking in prayer through the Passion as pilgrims did in Jerusalem, were then kept mostly in Franciscan churches. Leonard set them up wherever he went, some five hundred and seventy times by the usual count. In 1750, at the request of Pope Benedict XIV, he erected Stations inside the Colosseum, where Christians were thought to have died, and the Pope still prays the Way of the Cross there on Good Friday.
He died in Rome on 26 November 1751, at the friary of St. Bonaventure on the Palatine Hill, having come back from a mission worn out. He was beatified in 1796 and canonized in 1867.
why_here: The Stations of the Cross are a pilgrimage for people who cannot go to Jerusalem, and that is Leonard's gift to the whole Church. The Ave Maria Grotto works on the same idea. Br. Joseph Zoettl built small models of the shrines of the Holy Land and of Rome so that people in Alabama could see them, and pilgrims walk the hillside among them.

Leonard spent his life on missions, short and intense times of prayer and confession meant to start a person over. The abbey's Retreat and Conference Center, open since 1981, receives groups who come for something similar. His prayers belong to those guests, and to the monks who preach and hear confessions for them. His book on the Mass would serve a student preparing for Confirmation.
relic: One relic in the Gothic gilt reliquary of Franciscan saints, labelled "B. Leonardi a P[ortu Mauritio]", which calls him Blessed and so dates from before his canonization in 1867.
check: The number of Stations he erected (about 572) and the date of his patronage of parish missions (Pius XI, 1923) are the usual figures; worth a check.

name: St. Lucy
title: Virgin and martyr of Syracuse
summary: Lucy was a young Christian put to death at Syracuse in Sicily in the persecution of Diocletian. Her martyrdom is well attested, though the story of her life is mostly legend. Her name means light, and she is patron of the blind and of those with eye trouble, a simple saint to ask for the sight of students and older monks, and good company in the short December days before boarders go home.
life: Lucy was put to death at Syracuse in Sicily during the persecution of the Emperor Diocletian, the last and hardest of the Roman persecutions. That she was a real martyr is well attested. An inscription from the catacombs of Syracuse, from about a century after her death, already names her feast, and her name was put in the Roman Canon of the Mass early on, beside St. Agatha of Catania. Pope Gregory the Great knew her cult in the sixth century.

The story of her life was written later and is more legend than history. It says she was the daughter of a rich family, that her father died when she was young, and that her mother arranged her marriage to a pagan. Lucy took her mother, who suffered from bleeding, on pilgrimage to the tomb of St. Agatha at Catania. The mother was healed, and Lucy persuaded her to let her give her dowry to the poor. The young man she had refused was angry and denounced her as a Christian. The governor ordered her taken to a brothel, but, the story says, the guards could not move her, even with a team of oxen. Fire did not burn her, and she died by the sword.

Her name means "light", and her feast once fell near the shortest day of the year. So she became a saint of light in the dark of winter. In Sweden and elsewhere in Scandinavia, girls dressed in white with crowns of candles still keep her day. She also became the patron of the blind and of eyes. Later painters showed her holding her eyes on a dish, and a later legend says they were torn out, but that story is not in the early accounts and may have grown from her name and from the pictures.
Her body was taken from Syracuse to Constantinople and, after 1204, to Venice, where it lies in the church of San Geremia.
patronage: the blind and those with eye trouble
why_here: Students spend their days reading, at screens and in books, and many will need glasses before they finish school. St. Lucy, the patron of eyes, is a simple saint to ask for their sight, and for older monks whose eyes are failing in the infirmary or at their reading in choir.

Her feast also comes in mid-December, near the end of the fall term, when the days are short, exams are close and boarders are counting the days until they go home. A saint whose name means light is good company in that season.
relic: One relic in the medallion of the velvet case, labelled "s. Luciae V. M.", beside Sts. Francis, Anthony, Roch and Agatha.
check: The detail that her relics passed through Constantinople before Venice is the usual Venetian account; another tradition says they went to Metz.

name: St. Luke
title: Evangelist, physician, companion of St. Paul
summary: Luke wrote the Gospel that bears his name and the Acts of the Apostles, and St. Paul calls him "the beloved physician". Only his Gospel tells of the Annunciation, the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. He is patron of physicians and painters, the monks sing his three canticles every day, and his care as a historian suits Br. Leo's history books and students' research papers.
life: Luke wrote the Gospel that bears his name and its sequel, the Acts of the Apostles, which together make up more than a quarter of the New Testament. Both books are addressed to a man named Theophilus, and Luke says at the start that, since many had written accounts, he had looked carefully into everything from the beginning so as to write an orderly one. He wrote fine Greek and wrote as a historian, with dates and names of rulers.

St. Paul names him three times. He calls him "Luke, the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14), counts him among his fellow workers, and, writing from prison near the end, says, "Only Luke is with me". In Acts, some passages change from "they" to "we", and these are usually taken as the times Luke travelled with Paul, on the sea voyages to Macedonia and to Jerusalem, and on the voyage to Rome that ended in shipwreck on Malta. An early tradition says he was a Gentile from Antioch in Syria, that he never married, and that he died at eighty-four in Greece.

Much that Christians love best is found only in his Gospel. He alone tells of the angel coming to Mary, of the Visitation, of the shepherds and the manger, of the boy Jesus found in the Temple. He alone gives the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, the story of Zacchaeus, and the good thief on the cross. He pays close attention to the poor, to women, to outsiders and to prayer. He also preserved three canticles the Church has sung every day for centuries, Mary's Magnificat, Zechariah's Benedictus and Simeon's Nunc dimittis.

The story that he painted the Virgin Mary is a legend from several centuries later, but it made him the patron of painters. His body is venerated in the Benedictine basilica of Santa Giustina in Padua, and his head is kept in Prague.
why_here: The monks sing Luke's three canticles every day, the Benedictus at Lauds, the Magnificat at Vespers and the Nunc dimittis at Compline. He is in their mouths morning, evening and night.

He was a doctor, and the abbey has a long record of care for the sick. Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick in the yellow fever of 1878, Frater Hubert Carney died nursing others in 1918, and the monks keep an infirmary today. He was also a careful historian, a patron for Br. Leo's work on the abbey's history books, and for Prep students writing research papers who must, like Luke, check their sources first. The painters' patron fits a house of carvers and craftsmen too.
relic: One relic on the grey linen board, labelled "[S.] Lucae Evang.", "of St. Luke the Evangelist", in the same theca as a relic read as St. Patrick.
check: The relic of his head in Prague (St. Vitus Cathedral) is the usual claim; confirm if kept.

name: St. Maria Goretti
title: Virgin and martyr, patron of forgiveness
summary: Maria Goretti was an eleven-year-old Italian farm girl who was stabbed in 1902 by a young man, Alessandro Serenelli, when she refused his assault, and she forgave him before she died. Years later he repented and asked her mother's forgiveness. She is a patron of young people, especially teenage girls, and of forgiveness, and her story tells Prep students that their bodies and their consent matter.
life: Maria Goretti was born on 16 October 1890 at Corinaldo, near Ancona, the third of the children of Luigi and Assunta Goretti, poor farm workers. Looking for work, the family moved south, and by 1899 they were sharing a farmhouse at Le Ferriere, in the marshes near Nettuno, south of Rome, with another family, Giovanni Serenelli and his son Alessandro. The land was poor and the area full of malaria. In 1900 Maria's father died of it.

Assunta went out to work in the fields, and Maria, not yet ten, kept house, cooked, mended and minded the younger children. She could not read and had little schooling. She was devout, made her first Communion in 1901, and was known as a steady, cheerful girl.

Alessandro Serenelli, about twenty, began to press her for sex and threatened her. On 5 July 1902, when she was alone in the house, he tried to force her. She refused, telling him it was a sin and he would go to hell for it, and he stabbed her fourteen times. She was taken to the hospital at Nettuno and operated on without anesthetic. The next day, before she died, she said she forgave him and wanted him to be with her in heaven. She was eleven.

Serenelli was sentenced to thirty years in prison. For years he was unrepentant. Then, he said, he dreamed that Maria came to him in a garden and gave him lilies. He changed, and after his release in 1929 he went to Assunta and asked her forgiveness, and she gave it. They received Communion together at Christmas. He spent the rest of his life as a lay helper and gardener with the Capuchin friars, and died in 1970.

Pius XII beatified Maria in 1947 and canonized her in 1950 before an enormous crowd in St. Peter's Square, with her mother present. Serenelli was alive at the time. Her body is at the sanctuary of Our Lady of Graces in Nettuno.
why_here: Maria was a child who did a grown woman's work after her father died, and she was killed by a young man in her own house. Her story should be told to teenagers carefully and honestly. She is not a lesson that victims are to blame. She is a girl who knew her own worth and would not be used, and who was strong enough to forgive. Prep students living away from home, girls and boys alike, deserve to hear that their bodies and their consent matter, and her prayers serve that.

Her story is also Alessandro's. He was a young man who did a terrible thing, and with grace and the mercy of a mother he changed. Every school has to hold together justice for the harmed and hope for those who do wrong, and Maria and Assunta did both.
relic: One relic on the grey linen board, labelled "S. Maria Goretti V. M.", "St. Maria Goretti, Virgin and Martyr".
check: The year Serenelli asked Assunta's forgiveness is given variously (released 1929; the reconciliation and shared Communion at Christmas, often dated 1934 or 1937); I left the year out.

name: St. Martin of Tours (probably)
title: Soldier, monk and bishop
summary: The label says only "of Saint Martin", and this is most likely Martin of Tours, a Roman soldier who became a monk and then Bishop of Tours. His biographer tells how he cut his military cloak in half for a beggar, and that cloak gave us the word chaplain. He is a patron of soldiers and of the poor, a fitting saint for the abbey's military chaplains and for graduates in the services.
life: The label says only "S. Martini", "of Saint Martin". Martin of Tours, by far the most popular Martin, is the likely one, but it could be Pope St. Martin I, who died in exile in the Crimea in 655 after defending the faith against the emperor. Since there is no title on the label, the following is Martin of Tours.

Martin was born about 316 at Savaria in Pannonia, now Szombathely in Hungary, the son of a Roman army officer, and grew up at Pavia in northern Italy. Against his parents' wishes he became a catechumen as a boy. As an officer's son he was enrolled in the army at fifteen and served in a cavalry guard. His friend and biographer, Sulpicius Severus, tells the best known story. One bitter winter at Amiens, Martin met a beggar at the city gate, cut his military cloak in two with his sword, and gave the man half. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak and saying to the angels, "Martin, still a catechumen, has clothed me with this". He was baptized soon after.

Sulpicius says that before a battle Martin told his commander, "I am a soldier of Christ, I may not fight", and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy. He left the army and became a disciple of St. Hilary of Poitiers. About 361 he founded at Ligugé one of the first monasteries in Gaul. In 371 the people of Tours tricked him into the city and made him bishop against his will. He lived as a monk in a cell outside the city, where his community grew into the abbey of Marmoutier, and he travelled the countryside preaching, tearing down pagan shrines and founding parishes. He died on 8 November 397 at Candes and was buried at Tours on the 11th.

Sulpicius's Life is full of miracles, and some of it reads as legend, but it was written by a man who knew Martin. He was one of the first saints honored as a saint without being a martyr. The half-cloak, the cappa, was kept by the Frankish kings, and its keepers and the shrine where it was kept gave us the words chaplain and chapel.
why_here: Martin's half-cloak gave the Church the word chaplain, and monks of St. Bernard served as military chaplains in both world wars and in Korea. He was a soldier who became a monk, and a monk who was made to serve the wider Church, which describes those chaplains well. His prayers belong to Prep graduates who go into the services and to families of students in the military.

He has old ties to Benedictines too. St. Gregory tells that Benedict turned the temple of Apollo at Monte Cassino into an oratory of St. Martin. In German lands his feast is kept with lanterns and processions, a custom Cullman's German settlers would have known. And the saint who cut his cloak is a patron of tailors, a trade the monks still practice.
relic: One relic in a gilt sunburst with St. Andrew and one unread label, handwritten "S. Martini"; which Martin is not stated.
check: The label could be Pope St. Martin I (feast 13 April); only the authentica can settle it. The entry is written for Martin of Tours.

name: St. Martin de Porres
title: Dominican brother, barber and infirmarian
summary: Martin de Porres was a Dominican brother in Lima, Peru, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed woman of African descent, looked down on for his birth and his color. He served as barber, infirmarian and almoner, and he nursed the sick of the whole city. He is a patron of people of mixed race and of racial harmony, and of the abbey's brothers and charity among students from many backgrounds.
life: Martin was born in Lima, Peru, on 9 December 1579. His father, Juan de Porres, was a Spanish nobleman, and his mother, Ana Velázquez, was a freed woman of African descent from Panama. His baptismal record calls him the son of an unknown father, and for years his father did not acknowledge him. In the colonial society of Lima, a boy of mixed race and illegitimate birth stood near the bottom.

As a boy he was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon. In that time a barber cut hair, but he also pulled teeth, set bones, dressed wounds and let blood, and Martin learned to use herbs and medicines. At about fifteen he asked to join the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary in Lima. Men of his background could not then be full members, so he entered as a donado, a lay helper who did the servants' work. Some years later the community, impressed by him, had him make vows as a lay brother.

He was the community's barber, infirmarian and almoner, and he did the laundry and swept the floors. He nursed the sick friars, and then the sick of the city, Spanish, Indian and African, slave and free, sometimes bringing them into his own cell. He begged money from the rich and gave it to the poor, and he helped found a home and school for orphaned and abandoned children. He looked after stray cats and dogs, and the friary's farm animals. He was a friend of two other saints of Lima, St. Rose of Lima and St. John Macías.

Many wonders were told of him in his lifetime and after: that he was seen in two places at once, that he passed through locked doors, that he made peace among the mice in the priory. These belong to the tradition that grew up around him. What is plainly history is his humility and his care for everyone who came to the door.
He died on 3 November 1639. He was beatified in 1837 and canonized by John XXIII in 1962.
why_here: Martin was a brother, not a priest, and the abbey has always depended on its brothers. Among the monks' works the abbey lists barbering, the care of the sick in the infirmary, the farm with its cattle and chickens, the garden and the kitchen. Martin did all of these in Lima, and he is a natural patron for the brothers who do them at St. Bernard.

He is also a patron for a school whose students come from across the country and abroad. Martin was looked down on for the color of his skin and the circumstances of his birth, and he answered with service to everyone. Boarding schools put young people of very different backgrounds in the same halls, and he is a good saint to ask for charity among them. His feast falls in early November, in the month the Church remembers the dead.
relic: One relic on the grey linen board, handwritten "S. Martini de Porres", which calls him Saint and so was probably written in 1962 or later.
check: Pius XII is often said to have named him patron of social justice in Peru (1945); I left the pope out of the patronage list because I could not confirm it.

name: The Martyrs of Trier
title: Martyrs of the Roman city of Trier
summary: The Martyrs of Trier are Christians said to have been killed in that Roman city around 286 under the Emperor Maximian, soldiers of the Theban Legion and townspeople with them. The account was written centuries later and the huge numbers are legend, though martyrs at Trier are likely. They are patrons of Trier, and they come from the German lands that gave this abbey its monks.
life: Trier, on the Moselle in what is now western Germany, was one of the great cities of the late Roman Empire. Under Maximian, who shared the empire with Diocletian from 286, it became an imperial capital, and later Constantine lived there. It had a Christian community early, with bishops by the third century, St. Eucharius and St. Valerius among the first, by tradition.

The label reads "[Ex] Oss. Martirum Trevir[ensium] … sub imper. Maximiano et […] martirio coronati sunt", "from the bones of the Martyrs of Trier, … who were crowned with martyrdom under the Emperor Maximian and […]". The second name is hidden. The story it refers to says that around 286, under Maximian and his prefect Rictiovarus, soldiers of the Theban Legion, Christians from Egypt who had refused to sacrifice, were put to death at Trier, led by their officer Thyrsus. Then many citizens of the city, with their leader Palmatius, were killed for their faith as well, in such numbers that the Moselle was said to run red. Their remains are venerated in the crypt of the church of St. Paulinus in Trier.

How much of this is history is uncertain. The account as we have it was written down centuries later, in the Middle Ages, after bones were found at St. Paulinus. The Theban Legion story, best known from St. Maurice at Agaunum in Switzerland, was attached to several cities along the Rhine and Moselle, and the very large numbers are certainly legend. But Christians were persecuted under Maximian, and that there were martyrs at Trier is likely. The relic honors them, whoever and however many they were.
why_here: Trier's martyrs come from the German lands that gave this abbey its monks. Metten in Bavaria sent monks to St. Vincent, St. Vincent sent them to Cullman, and Cullman itself was founded by German immigrants. Trier's Benedictine abbey of St. Matthias still keeps the tombs of its first bishops, and this relic hangs beside another "from the holy relics of the Abbey of St. Matthias".

The story's heroes are soldiers who would not betray their conscience and ordinary townspeople who stood with them. That is a fair picture of what the Church asks of lay people, the oblates and families of the abbey among them, when faith costs something.
relic: One relic in the set of jewelled gilt reliquaries, labelled "[Ex] Oss. Martirum Trevir[ensium] … sub imper. Maximiano et […] martirio coronati sunt".
check: The catalogue marks the reading as probable. The names Thyrsus and Palmatius, the medieval date of the written account (often tied to a discovery of bones at St. Paulinus in 1072), and the local feast day (early October at Trier) should be checked before publishing.
